rationale: Synthesizes Ferry's speech with the Africa map to show moral 'duty' language masked strategic/economic motives; the task is explaining how the source's claims function as justification for empire.
Asks how Ferry's 'duty of superior races' claim differs from earlier justifications; requires explaining how his argument modifies/refutes prior religious and dynastic rationales for empire.

Asks which broader context explains the rapid 1880s-1900s partition; the student identifies industrial-era technologies (steamships, quinine, repeating rifles) as the enabling context for the Scramble for Africa.
Uses the coal/steamship charts as evidence to explain Meiji industrialization as a deliberate state project; the task is explaining how the evidence supports that claim.
Interprets what the emphasis on coal and steamships reveals — Meiji Japan building military-industrial power to revise the unequal treaties, an indigenous response to Western state expansion.
Explains the charts' steep curves via the late-developer advantage of adopting proven foreign technologies; a claim about how industrialization spread.
Interprets the 1894-95 victory as evidence of Japan's arrival as a modern military power against Qing China — Japan's own state expansion.
Interprets the 1905 victory's significance as inspiration for anti-colonial nationalists across Asia and Africa — an indigenous response to European state expansion.
Uses Auclert's account as evidence refuting France's 'civilizing mission' rationale for empire in Algeria.
Asks what Auclert's blaming of both French officials and conservative Muslim men reveals about her argument's point of view — a feminist critique of the colonial civilizing-mission rationale.
Uses Auclert's observation of pre-1830 girls' schools as evidence that indigenous Algerian institutions predated and were dismantled by French state expansion.

Asks what the petitioners' choice of audience (merchants, humble tone) reveals about their historical situation — disenfranchised workers with no vote or unions. Topic fit is weak: this is a Unit 5-style labor item filed in Unit 6; 6.4 is the closest available.
Explains the evidence — machines spread despite protests because they slashed labor costs and gave adopters a competitive advantage.

Analyzes the petition's deferential tone and appeal to conscience as the petitioners' rhetorical purpose and strategy toward their audience. Same weak Unit-6 topic fit as u6-023; 6.4 is the closest available.
Situates the 1786 petition within the broader context of worker resistance to mechanization, showing it predated the Luddite risings by a generation.
Situates Rodney's 1974 argument within the postcolonial debate over genuine economic independence, arguing that European imperialism actively underdeveloped Africa.
Explains the swadeshi boycott as a response to British factory cloth destroying Indian handlooms — a claim about economic imperialism's effects.
Analyzes Komatsu's purpose and audience — persuading Western readers that Japan's annexation of Korea was natural and beneficial; the content is Japan's rise as a power after 1900.

Identifies the anthem's claim that Pakistan's founding ideology required a separate Muslim homeland. Filed in Unit 7 though the content (partition nationalism) fits Unit 8 decolonization topics better; 7.1 is the closest available.
Explains Berryman's point of view — American cartoonists depicting Mussolini as Hitler's boastful junior partner on the eve of WWII.
Identifies the claim that Mussolini and Hitler reached power through appointment and maneuvering rather than direct election — part of the causes of WWII.
Uses the 1935 invasion of Ethiopia as evidence exposing the League of Nations' inability to stop aggression by a major power — a cause of WWII.
Analyzes Nicholas II's framing of forced abdication as patriotic sacrifice — the tsar's point of view and purpose in the 1917 collapse of imperial power.
Identifies the tension in Lenin's claim of seizing power 'on behalf of' the soviets while acting as a minority party — the argument's central contradiction.
Identifies the immediate historical context of the September 1, 1939 speech — delivered as Germany invaded Poland, with Versailles grievances as rhetorical cover.
Compares the main ideas of two wartime speeches — both leaders framing their cause in moral absolutes to mobilize their peoples for total war.
Analyzes Stalin's rhetorical purpose — reciting Russia's historical humiliations to spur industrial managers into the breakneck pace of the Five-Year Plans.
Explains what the speech's audience of industrial managers reveals about Stalin's campaign — enlisting the technical elite in the industrialization drive.
Identifies the claim in Stalin's 'jungle law of capitalism' phrase — international relations as a predatory struggle requiring Soviet strength.
Analyzes the tension in Stalin's point of view — fusing Marxist economic goals with Russian nationalist pride to motivate industrialization.
Uses the GDP table as evidence that American bombing and military defeat devastated the Japanese economy between 1944 and 1946.
Uses the GDP table as evidence that military expansion and war production drove Japan's measured economic growth from 1934 to 1942.
Asks what limitation of the GDP data a historian must recognize — economic figures alone cannot capture the war's total human cost.
Situates Nkrumah's 1961 speech within the decolonization-era debate over whether new African states should unite in federation or go their separate ways.
Explains how Nkrumah's 'not won at the expense of others' claim functions — a deliberate contrast with the exploitative European imperialism he opposes.
Asks what limitation of the speech a historian must recognize — it reveals Nkrumah's aspirations, not the political realities or obstacles among African leaders.
Explains how the OAU's outcome modifies Nkrumah's federal vision — it became an association of sovereign states because members refused to surrender their new independence.
Identifies the anthem's claim that Pakistani national identity is defined through Islamic faith rather than ethnicity or language.
Situates the 1954 anthem's adoption within the broader context of new postcolonial states using national symbols to forge unity among diverse populations.
Uses the anthem as a springboard to explain partition's most significant long-term consequence — disputed borders, notably Kashmir, producing lasting conflict.

Analyzes what Berryman's 1938 cartoon reveals about the US historical situation — American contempt for fascist Italy alongside official neutrality. Weak Unit-8 fit (pre-WWII content); 8.1 is the closest available.
Uses the 1960 summit exchange as evidence that even face-to-face summits could collapse when espionage destroyed trust between the superpowers.
Analyzes what Eisenhower's 'distasteful necessity' phrasing reveals — an unusually frank US admission of espionage as a deliberate tool of national security.
Analyzes Khrushchev's purpose and audience — competing with the United States for moral authority before world public opinion.
Explains how Khrushchev's 'peaceful co-existence' claim breaks with the Stalin-era assumption that war between capitalist and socialist systems was inevitable.
Analyzes the GLF manifesto's point of view — demanding that gay men sacrifice their own male chauvinism and privilege, turning the movement's critique inward.
Situates NOW's 1966 statement within the broader context of the 1960s global wave of movements challenging established hierarchies.
Compares the two sources' main ideas — NOW's pursuit of institutional integration versus the GLF's pursuit of transformation of the gender system itself.
Identifies the shared historical context of both sources — the 1960s-70s wave of movements (civil rights, feminism, gay liberation) challenging established hierarchies.
Identifies the claim in Ho's 1930 address — a revolutionary strategy of uniting workers, peasants, soldiers, and youth under communist leadership.
Explains how the program's claims work together — national independence and confiscation of banks and plantations presented as one inseparable struggle, not two separate goals.
Identifies Gandhi's strategic claim — linking the Khilafat cause with swaraj to merge Muslim and Hindu grievances into one mass anti-colonial front.
Identifies the satyagraha principle in 'earn imprisonment' — willingly suffering unjust punishment to expose the injustice of British rule.
Uses the source to explain how WWII bankrupted Britain and spurred anti-colonial movements, making the empire unaffordable and indefensible.
Uses the GDP table as evidence that Japanese output per person only just regained prewar levels by 1955 — a decade of postwar recovery under the Cold War order.
Explains the significance of Article 5 — committing the United States to Europe's peacetime defense and breaking 150 years of tradition against permanent alliances.
Analyzes the treaty's purpose in repeatedly invoking the UN Charter — framing NATO as lawful self-defense under international norms rather than an aggressive bloc.
Identifies the historical context of the 1949 treaty — the Berlin Blockade and growing Soviet power making Western military cooperation urgent.
Explains how NATO's collective-defense pledge changed small member states' strategic position — gaining American protection they could never provide for themselves.

Identifies the claim linking Troyes (1420) to the Berlin Conference — sovereignty over people transferred by outside diplomats without consulting inhabitants. Filed in Unit 9 though the content is imperial-era; 9.9 continuity/change is the closest available.

Identifies the pooling of European sovereignty through economic and political union as the postwar development rejecting the song's exclusive blood-and-soil nationalism — a globalized-world institution.

Analyzes what Mansa Musa's depiction on a European-made map reveals about the source's historical situation — Mali's gold wealth was known around the Mediterranean via trans-Saharan networks after the 1324 pilgrimage.
Identifies the claim the map supports — Mali's economic power rested on controlling the overland routes linking the southern goldfields to the northern caravan cities.
Identifies the development the map shows — the Delhi Sultanate c. 1330 as a Muslim-ruled state controlling nearly the entire Indian subcontinent.
Identifies the claim the Qutb Minar supports — new Muslim rulers proclaiming authority through monumental Islamic architecture inscribed in Arabic.
Identifies the claim the map labels support — the Mongol Empire had divided into separate khanates, with the Yuan ruling China as one of them.
Analyzes what the Chinese-style Nanjing map reveals about the source's situation — Chinese urban, cartographic, and administrative traditions continued under Yuan rule.
Identifies the claim the coins support — the Mongol Yuan rulers adopted existing Chinese monetary practices (round cash coins with square holes).
Analyzes what the court painting reveals — the Yuan elite kept Mongol steppe customs like the ritual hunt while ruling China, a dual identity.
Identifies the claim the map's western boundary supports — the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt halted the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut in 1260.
Explains the Inca road system's function — letting Cuzco move officials, armies, and supplies quickly across a mountainous empire with no writing or wheel.
Identifies the claim the Machu Picchu photograph supports — Inca engineering of agricultural terraces and mortarless stonework suited to steep Andean slopes.
Identifies the development the quipu represents — an Inca record-keeping system for taxes and census data that needed no written script.
Identifies the claim the Codex Mendoza tribute page supports — the Aztec Empire extracted wealth, including luxury craft goods, from its provinces.
Identifies the Mexica cultural feature the image shows — priest-scholars (tlamatini) studying the stars, knowledge used for the calendar and rituals.
Identifies the claim the map supports — the Aztecs controlled central Mexico directly and ruled distant peoples mainly through tribute, not direct administration.
Identifies the Maya adaptation the site plan supports — settling around cenote groundwater sources in a limestone land with almost no surface rivers.
Identifies the claim Angkor Wat supports — Khmer kings displaying power and legitimizing rule through monumental Hindu temples built as Mount Meru.
Identifies the pattern the map shows — mainland Southeast Asia c. 1200 held several large competing regional states (Khmer, Pagan, Dai Viet), not one united empire.
Identifies the long-distance process Borobudur illustrates — Buddhism spreading from India to Southeast Asia along maritime trade routes and being monumentalized by local rulers.
Identifies the claim the legend and shading support — Majapahit as a maritime empire controlling the sea lanes and straits of the Indonesian archipelago.
Identifies the claim the mosque's materials and style support — Islam in West Africa blending with local building traditions and materials (adobe, toron beams).
Identifies the claim the ruins support — a wealthy indigenous African state mobilizing organized labor for monumental dry-stone walls, funded by the gold trade.
Identifies the claim the rock church supports — a powerful indigenous African Christian kingdom (Ethiopia) capable of monumental architecture.
Explains the plague's spread pattern — traveling along trade routes and entering Europe through its busiest ports, with spared areas lying off the main routes.
Explains why Silk Road travel became safer in the 1200s-1300s — Mongol conquests placed most of the route under one political umbrella (the Pax Mongolica).
Explains the connection — Muslim scholars advanced astronomy, and instruments like the astrolabe embodied and spread that knowledge to other regions.
Judges the image's limitation as a source — a 15th-century French artist's imagining of the Mongol court, evidence of how Europeans imagined Asia rather than a literal record.

Identifies the claim the Alhambra supports — the Nasrid emirate as the last Muslim state in Iberia, ruling from a fortified palace-city. Placed in Dar al-Islam rather than Europe since the development is Muslim Iberia.
Identifies the claim the castle supports — European Christians establishing fortified Crusader states in the eastern Mediterranean (Krak des Chevaliers as a Hospitaller headquarters).
Identifies the claim the mosque's scale and decoration support — Timur's conquest state turning plunder and tribute into imperial Islamic monuments.
Identifies the Korean response the printing blocks illustrate — commissioning a vast Buddhist canon as spiritual defense while Mongol armies invaded Korea.
Identifies the claim the Cliff Palace photograph supports — Ancestral Puebloan cliff-alcove villages with kivas showing organized communal religious life.
Identifies the claim Monks Mound supports — a complex Mississippian society able to mobilize massive labor for the largest pre-Columbian earthwork north of Mexico.
Identifies the pattern Ibn Battuta's route illustrates — a connected Muslim world of shared faith and law in which one traveler could reach from Morocco to India.
Identifies the development the map shows — late medieval northern European commerce run by a league of self-governing merchant cities, not a single kingdom.
Identifies the pattern — overland and maritime routes formed overlapping networks connecting distant Afro-Eurasian regions, not a single road.
Identifies the exchange the map's labels and arrows characterize — Saharan salt moving south into West Africa while gold moved north to the Mediterranean.
Identifies the claim about trans-Saharan organization — routes linked West African goldfields to North African cities through intermediate oasis and market towns.
Identifies the connection — Mali integrated into interregional networks radiating north to the Mediterranean, northeast to Egypt, and east toward the Red Sea.
Identifies the claim the banknote supports — the Yuan state issued standardized paper currency, lowering the cost and risk of large-scale commerce.
Identifies what the printing block's existence indicates — Yuan paper currency was mass-produced with printing technology so the state could issue uniform notes.
Explains the connection — Rubruck's 1253-55 journey illustrates that Mongol rule made Asian travel safe for European travelers (the Pax Mongolica).
Identifies the claim the map supports — four politically divided khanates still forming a continuous Mongol-ruled zone across Eurasia c. 1300.
Analyzes what the Ilkhanid-court miniature's historical situation reveals — Mongols adopted siege technology (traction trebuchets) from conquered sedentary peoples.
Identifies the Mongol policy the paiza illustrates — the government issued safe-conduct passes protecting travelers and encouraging long-distance trade.
Identifies the claim the illustration supports — Chinese ocean-going junks sailed the sea routes between China and Southeast Asia.
Identifies the development the journey illustrates — Ibn Battuta's route stayed almost entirely within Dar al-Islam, showing Islam's connected zone across Africa and Asia.
Identifies the development — Mali's cities linked to North Africa by caravan routes through Taghaza, integrating Mali into trans-Saharan trade networks.
Identifies the claim the Stahlhof inset supports — Hanseatic merchants maintained permanent, self-governing trading enclaves in foreign cities like London.
Identifies the pattern the color-coded routes show — Asian goods reached Europe via Alexandria and the Black Sea while the Hansa ran northern trade, a division of commercial labor.
Identifies the feature the ducat illustrates — Venice created a trusted high-value gold currency to serve its long-distance eastern commerce.

Analyzes what the fortress's historical situation reveals — Italian merchants kept fortified trading colonies on the Black Sea, the western terminus of the Silk Road routes linking Asia and the Mediterranean.
Identifies the claim the Djinguereber Mosque supports — Islam in Mali expressed through local West African building traditions rather than imported Arab forms.

Identifies the development the Qutb Minar illustrates in a Unit-2 frame — Turkic Muslim rulers establishing authority in northern India through Islamic monuments, a cultural consequence of connectivity.
Identifies the phenomenon — Muslim merchants forming settled communities, with a mosque, in the Chinese port city of Quanzhou.
Analyzes what the stele's situation reveals — Christianity spread to Tang China along Silk Road networks and took Chinese artistic forms.
Identifies the claim the aerial view supports — a wealthy, organized African society sustained by the gold trade feeding into the Indian Ocean world.
Identifies the feature the Kilwa coins illustrate — Swahili city-states with sophisticated commercial economies that minted their own coinage.
Identifies the connection the mosque interior supports — Islam rooted on the Swahili coast, where Indian Ocean trade wealth built great mosques.

Identifies the claim Bete Giyorgis supports — Ethiopia's distinctive, independent Christian tradition. The Unit-2 fit is loose (Ethiopian Christianity predates these networks), but 2.5 is the closest available topic.
Identifies the cultural-exchange claim Angkor Wat supports — Indian Hindu religious and architectural ideas adopted and monumentalized in Southeast Asia.
Identifies the exchange aspect the David Vases illustrate — Chinese luxury porcelain depended on interregional trade, with Persian cobalt producing the blue decoration.

Explains the connection — Mamluk astronomical and navigational technology was later adopted by Europeans and aided sea trade. Framed as a cultural/technological consequence of connectivity (2.5); 2.3 was the alternative.
Identifies the claim the Java cannon supports — Chinese gunpowder weapons diffused to Java in the Mongol era.
Identifies the development the Yuan hand-cannon illustrates — gunpowder weapons developed in China and later spreading westward across Eurasia.
Analyzes what the Japanese scroll's situation reveals — the Mongols used gunpowder bombs against Japan, but the invasions failed, showing the limits of Mongol expansion.
Analyzes what the portrait's situation reveals — Mongol rulers adopted Chinese imperial artistic conventions to legitimize their dynasty in China.
Identifies the development the court painting illustrates — the Yuan court keeping Mongol steppe traditions while ruling China, with cultures in close contact.
Judges the engraving's limitation as a source — made three centuries after Polo's death, it reflects later European imagination rather than his actual appearance.

Identifies the development the celadon illustrates — Korea producing luxury goods and taking part in East Asian exchange networks. 2.1 is approximate, since the CED exchange topics center on the Silk Roads and Indian Ocean.
Uses the siege map as evidence to explain the 1453 Ottoman success — massive gunpowder artillery against the land walls plus hauling ships overland into the Golden Horn.
Identifies the claim the defender-sector names suggest — Constantinople's defense depended on Western European soldiers, showing how far Byzantine power had shrunk before Ottoman expansion.
Explains Mohács in its broader context — Ottoman gunpowder weapons and a large, disciplined standing army giving them decisive advantage over Hungary.
Analyzes the Huenername's purpose — Ottoman rulers using lavish official illustrated histories to celebrate conquests and legitimize the dynasty's claim to universal empire.
Identifies the Ottoman institution the janissary represents — the devshirme system recruiting Christian youths as the sultan's full-time standing infantry.

Analyzes what the janissary's appearance in a 1590 Venetian costume book reveals — Europeans closely observed Ottoman military power because it mattered in European politics and trade. A weaker fit, placed in the comparison topic.
Identifies the Ottoman governmental feature the gate's graded courts reflect — power concentrated in the sultan's household, with access to the ruler graded by rank and function.
Analyzes what the French manuscript's production reveals — the fall of Constantinople alarmed Western Christians, who saw the Ottoman advance as a grave threat to Christendom.
Analyzes what the sultan's inclusion in the Medici portrait collection reveals — European rulers regarded the Ottoman sultan as a major world power worth studying and collecting.
Identifies the development the campaign belongs to — the long Ottoman-Safavid struggle for control of the Caucasus and the eastern frontier lands.
Explains the bombard's significance to Ottoman expansion — giant gunpowder artillery battering down the massive stone walls of fortified cities such as Constantinople.
Identifies the development Chaldiran exemplifies — Ottoman muskets and field artillery defeating a Safavid cavalry army, a turning point in the Ottoman-Safavid rivalry.
Explains how the miniature's claims work — Safavid court artists commemorated even a defeat by centering Shah Ismail heroically, showing dynastic histories reshaping the past to honor the founder.
Identifies the Safavid policy the mosque reflects — the shahs fusing royal and religious authority, making Twelver Shi'ism the ideological foundation of the state.
Identifies what the carpet's destination reflects — Safavid rulers cultivating their Sufi ancestors' shrines as sources of dynastic legitimacy.
Analyzes what the portraits' creation reveals — active diplomatic contact between the Mughal and Safavid courts, with artists accompanying embassies to record the rival ruler's likeness.
Identifies the Mughal imperial claim the composition reflects — Jahangir presented as a universal sovereign whose spiritual legitimacy outranked even foreign kings.
Identifies the connection the Ottoman and English figures reflect — the Mughal court knew of and contacted distant powers, the Ottomans to the west and the English seeking trading privileges.
Analyzes the painting's purpose — Mughal court propaganda projecting Jahangir as the greater sovereign graciously receiving a rival during an uneasy rivalry with Persia.
Explains how the Mughals governed their vast empire — a centralized administration assessing and collecting land revenue from rich agricultural lands, funding the army and court.

Identifies the conclusion the map's southern limit supports — despite maximum extent, the empire never fully subdued the subcontinent, and endless Deccan campaigns strained resources (limits of expansion).
Identifies the imperial strategy the hall's open design reflects — cultivating the emperor's image as an accessible dispenser of justice to legitimize rule over a diverse population.
Identifies what the gateway's enormous scale reflects — Akbar using monumental architecture to advertise military victory and project imperial power over newly conquered regions.
Identifies what the saying of Jesus on the gateway evidences — Akbar's sulh-i kul policy of religious inclusivity, drawing wisdom from multiple religious traditions.
Identifies what the court's production of the painting reflects — projecting the emperor's personal courage and mastery over the wild as proof of fitness to rule.

Analyzes what the portrait reveals — elite Mughal women wielding public, even sovereign-style power (Nur Jahan issuing orders, hunting as a royal prerogative). Placed in legitimacy/belief-systems since it concerns sovereign prerogatives; the fit is loose.
Explains the problem the image illustrates — overextension: endless Deccan wars drained the treasury and kept the emperor from the capital, straining administration.
Identifies the Mughal feature the durbar's formal arrangement reflects — court ritual displaying a strict hierarchy centered on the emperor, through whom honors and patronage flowed.
Identifies what the armored equestrian portrait reflects — Qing rulers preserving and advertising their Manchu martial identity while adopting Chinese imperial institutions.
Identifies the Qing legitimation strategy the portrait reflects — presenting the Manchu emperor as a Confucian sage-ruler mastering Chinese cultural symbols.
Identifies the Chinese imperial concept the hall reflects — the emperor as the Son of Heaven, with palace architecture expressing cosmic centrality and supreme ritual authority.
Identifies what the Qing preservation of the Ming throne hall illustrates — the Manchu conquerors legitimizing rule by adopting Ming imperial ritual and institutions rather than replacing them.
Explains the Ming wall investment — the need to defend against raids and invasions by Mongol and other steppe peoples along the northern frontier.
Analyzes what the map's existence reveals — Jesuits serving the Qing court as astronomers and cartographers, with their surveys published in Europe and deepening European knowledge of China.
Explains the factor in Russia's eastward expansion the painting illustrates — firearms giving small Russian forces a decisive advantage over bow-armed Siberian peoples.
Identifies what the Orthodox banners suggest — Russian expansion framed as a Christian mission, with conquest and conversion marching together to justify conquest.
Identifies what St. Basil's construction reflects — Ivan IV using Orthodox Christianity and victory monuments to legitimize the tsar's expanding autocratic power.
Identifies the claims the portrait's symbols make — the tsar as autocratic ruler and defender of Orthodox Christianity, Moscow as the 'Third Rome' succeeding Byzantium.
Explains the streltsy suppression as Petrine policy — destroying the old Muscovite military elite to centralize autocratic power and clear the way for a Western-style army.
Identifies what the portrait's Western style reflects — Peter deliberately adopting Western military and cultural models to transform Russia into a European great power.
Identifies the Petrine goal the background ships point to — building a navy and gaining sea access through the Great Northern War against Sweden and the founding of St. Petersburg.
Judges the engraving's limitation as a source — even as contact grew, Europeans' direct knowledge of Japan stayed thin, so images of its rulers relied on hearsay and imagination.
Identifies the strategy Hideyoshi's court-dress portrait reflects — legitimizing his rule by obtaining high imperial court ranks, since his low birth barred him from the shogun title.
Identifies the purpose the shrine's extravagant decoration served — fusing religious reverence with political authority so that loyalty to the Tokugawa house carried divine sanction.
